# CAFE: Confining Feature Distillation to Language-Routed Adapters for Compact Multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition

**Authors:** Tianchi Liu Nicholas Moratelli Khurram Azeem Hashmi Affiliation: Mohammadreza Zolfaghari, Rishabh Jain, Louis Lu, Changdae Park, Amril Nazir Affiliation: Tether AI Research

## Abstract

Feature distillation is usually expected to add to logit distillation. We find that this expectation does not hold for two common feature losses in compact multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR), and analyze why through their gradients. The gradient of a projection-based loss is orthogonal to the task gradient, while that of Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), a similarity-based loss, is weakly aligned with it. CKA lowers the word error rate (WER) on non-English languages, but at the expense of data-rich English. Three loss-level remedies (one trained, two probed) all fall short, and the CKA gradient overlaps with the subspace English uses in the shared encoder by 97.5% to 99.5% (about 81% by chance). Guided by this diagnosis, we propose CAFE (Confined-Adapter Feature distillation), which confines the CKA gradient to adapters that English bypasses, addressing the trade-off in the parameters rather than in the loss. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, CAFE lowers the average WER from 8.55% to 8.02%, beats an adapter-only capacity control at 8.51%, and makes English more stable across checkpoints. At 254M parameters, it trails the 0.6B teacher by 2 WER points and is competitive with much larger models across 48 test sets in 24 languages. We use 564k hours of training data and state-of-the-art models to keep the findings relevant to practice.11 1 Checkpoints and usage instructions are available at https://huggingface.co/qvac/TranscribePsy-250M-EU. TranscribePsy-250M-EU is the 25-language CAFE model.

## 1 Introduction

*Figure 1: Averaged English and Multilingual WER vs. model size on the Open ASR Leaderboard.*

Automatic speech recognition (ASR) increasingly calls for one model that transcribes many languages, letting high-resource languages transfer to low-resource ones (Radford et al., 2023; Pratap et al., 2024). Such a model must serve data-rich English and a long tail of lower-resource languages at the same time, and the gap between them persists (Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2026). Many applications also need the model to run on device, for privacy, low latency, and offline use (Jeffries et al., 2024; Kudlur et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025b; Kamahori et al., 2025; Hashmi et al., 2026). A compact student performs better when initialized by structured pruning of a strong teacher rather than at random (Zhang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026) and trained with logit distillation from it (Hinton et al., 2015; Gandhi et al., 2023).

Many works also match intermediate features (Romero et al., 2015; Zagoruyko and Komodakis, 2017; Park et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2020), and speech encoders are often compressed this way (Chang et al., 2024a; Zampierin et al., 2024; Chi et al., 2025), on the assumption that a feature loss adds useful signal beyond the logits. In a multilingual model, however, all languages share one encoder, and a signal that helps some languages can hurt others (Chang et al., 2024b). Whether feature distillation still adds to logit distillation in this setting, and why, is not well understood.

This paper first diagnoses why feature distillation fails in this setting, and then uses the diagnosis to fix it. We distill a compact multilingual ASR student, initialized by structured pruning of the teacher, and find that neither of two common feature losses adds to logit distillation: a projection-based loss has almost no effect, and Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) (Cortes et al., 2012; Kornblith et al., 2019), a similarity-based loss, trades English for the non-English languages. To find out why, we analyze the gradient that each loss sends to the encoder. The projection-based gradient is orthogonal to the task, while the CKA gradient acts on the same encoder directions that English uses. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose Confined-Adapter Feature distillation (CAFE), which applies the CKA loss only through adapters that English bypasses and stops its gradient from reaching the shared encoder. Our contributions are:

- • Analysis. We show that two common feature losses do not add to logit distillation in compact multilingual ASR, and use their gradients to explain why (Sections 4.1 and 4.2).

- • Diagnosis. The multilingual CKA gradient overlaps with the subspace English uses by 97.5–99.5% (about 81% by chance), which explains why masking English in the loss fails and argues against two other loss-level remedies (Section 4.3).

- • Method. CAFE separates the trade-off in the parameters rather than in the loss, so feature distillation no longer comes at the expense of English (Section 5).

- • Results. CAFE’s gains over the baselines come mainly from English, with a smaller multilingual gain. It beats a capacity control with the same adapters but no feature loss, and halves the variation of English WER across checkpoints. At 254M parameters it is 2 WER points behind the 0.6B teacher (Section 7).

## 2 Related Work

#### Logit and feature distillation.

Knowledge distillation matches a student’s outputs to a teacher’s (Hinton et al., 2015). Feature-based variants add intermediate signal by matching activations (Romero et al., 2015; Zagoruyko and Komodakis, 2017) or relations among examples (Park et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2020), and a parallel line improves the logit term (Zhao et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2022). It is commonly assumed that a feature term helps on top of a logit term. In our setting, we find this does not hold for two common feature losses.

#### Representational similarity and CKA.

CKA (Cortes et al., 2012) became a standard tool for comparing neural representations across models of different width and initialization (Kornblith et al., 2019). Recent work also uses it as a training loss between models of different dimensions, with positive results, including in multilingual settings (Dasgupta and Cohn, 2025). Other feature distillation methods, such as VkD (Miles et al., 2024), project the student into the teacher space, or match layers with a contrastive loss to compress multilingual speech encoders (Chang et al., 2024a). We use similar losses but reach different conclusions, mainly because of the setting: a compact multilingual ASR student initialized by pruning, trained with strong logit distillation, on large-scale data dominated by English. Here, a VkD-style projection loss has almost no effect, and CKA helps only the languages with fewer resources compared with English. We limit these claims to multilingual ASR.

#### Multilingual ASR distillation.

Distillation is a standard way to compress speech models, through pseudo labels (Gandhi et al., 2023; Waheed et al., 2025) or dual-mode multilingual encoders (Male et al., 2025). Della Libera et al. (2024) benchmark adding languages to a multilingual model without catastrophic forgetting. Closest to us, Ferraz et al. (2024) add language-specific gated experts to a distilled Whisper Radford et al. (2023) student to raise per-language accuracy. Our adapters serve a different purpose. They are not there to add capacity, but to keep a feature distillation gradient inside the adapters and away from the shared encoder.

#### Adapters and conditional computation.

Bottleneck adapters (Houlsby et al., 2019) and low-rank updates Hu et al. (2022) adapt a frozen backbone, and language-specific adapters improve multilingual performance without disturbing other languages (Bapna and Firat, 2019; Pfeiffer et al., 2020). Recent work selects language-specific LoRA experts with the model’s own language identification (Kwok et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a), or studies bottleneck adapters for low-resource ASR (Samin et al., 2025; Dahal et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Oukid et al., 2026). In these works the adapter is used for transfer, while we use it to restrict where a distillation gradient can act.

#### When distillation helps or hurts.

Matching the teacher more closely does not always improve generalization (Stanton et al., 2021), and a stronger teacher can produce a worse student (Busbridge et al., 2025). Our finding is in the same spirit, applied to feature matching. When a feature loss conflicts with the task, gradient surgery projects the conflicting gradients apart (Yu et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2025). In our case, this would barely help, as the gradients are orthogonal rather than opposed. This is why we separate them in the parameters.

## 3 Preliminaries

We distill Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 Sekoyan et al. (2025); Xu et al. (2023); Rekesh et al. (2023) into a 254M student, initialized by structured pruning of the teacher Muralidharan et al. (2024). We report WER on the Open ASR Leaderboard (Srivastav et al., 2025): EN-7 and ML-9 summarize its seven English and nine multilingual sets. We evaluate each system with checkpoint averaging (CA) Polyak and Juditsky (1992); Vaswani et al. (2017), which averages the weights of its last 7 checkpoints. Section 6 gives the full details.

The training objective combines a supervised transducer loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{sup}}$ , logit distillation $\mathcal{L}_{\text{logit}}$ , and an optional feature distillation loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{feat}}$ ,

$$ \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{sup}}+\lambda_{\text{logit}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{logit}}+\lambda_{\text{feat}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{feat}}, $$

where the $\lambda$ terms are loss weights. The logit term is the KL divergence between student and teacher label and duration distributions at temperature $\tau$ ,

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{logit}}=\tau^{2}\sum_{c}p^{T}_{c}\big(\log p^{T}_{c}-\log p^{S}_{c}\big), $$

summed over the label and duration heads. We call the recipe with $\lambda_{\text{feat}}{=}0$ the Baseline.

*Figure 2: Feature-only runs: the same supervised recipe plus one feature distillation loss, with logit distillation off. (a) Feature loss (log scale). (b) The same loss divided by its initial value. (c) Wall-clock time per training step. VkD w/o norm is the projection loss without LayerNorm.*

Given student features $S\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{s}}$ and teacher features $T\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{t}}$ over $N$ valid frames ( $d_{s}{=}640$ , $d_{t}{=}1024$ ), we compare two types of loss for $\mathcal{L}_{\text{feat}}$ . The first is a VkD-style projection loss (Miles et al., 2024), called VkD variant in our tables. A projection $P$ with orthonormal columns ( $P^{\top}P{=}I$ ) maps the student to the teacher dimension, $\hat{S}{=}SP^{\top}$ , and a LayerNorm without affine parameters ( $\mathrm{LN}$ ) is applied to both $\hat{S}$ and the teacher before matching them frame by frame,

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{VkD}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n}\tfrac{1}{d_{t}}\big\|\tilde{S}_{n}-\tilde{T}_{n}\big\|_{2}^{2}, $$

with $\tilde{S}=\mathrm{LN}(\hat{S})$ and $\tilde{T}=\mathrm{LN}(T)$ ; the w/o norm variant omits the LayerNorm. The second is linear CKA (Cortes et al., 2012; Kornblith et al., 2019), which compares the similarity structure of the two feature sets, needs no projection, and works with $d_{s}\neq d_{t}$ ,

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{CKA}}=1-\frac{\|\bar{S}^{\top}\bar{T}\|_{F}^{2}}{\|\bar{S}^{\top}\bar{S}\|_{F}\,\|\bar{T}^{\top}\bar{T}\|_{F}}, $$

where $\bar{S},\bar{T}$ are column centered, and the loss is averaged over the distilled layers (Section 6).

## 4 Analysis: When and Why Feature Distillation Helps or Hurts

### 4.1 Which feature loss actually trains the student?

We first check whether each feature loss changes the student at all. We run three feature-only probes with logit distillation off, identical except for the feature loss, so the loss curve shows directly whether the optimizer can reduce it.

#### The projection loss stalls, while CKA keeps decreasing.

Figure 2 shows the feature loss and the step time. The projection loss, with or without LayerNorm, stops decreasing right after warmup, while CKA keeps falling, to about a quarter of its initial value (panel b). This is not specific to the probes: in the full recipe with logit distillation, the projection loss stays flat from step 49 to the end of training.

| feature term | $\\|g_{\text{feat}}\\|/\\|g_{\text{sup}}\\|$ | $\cos(g_{\text{feat}},g_{\text{sup}})$ |
|---|---|---|
| VkD variant | $7.3\times 10^{-4}$ | $+0.009$ |
| VkD w/o norm | $0.15$ | $-0.005$ |
| CKA | $1.1\times 10^{-3}$ | $+0.087$ |

*Table 1: Median ratio of gradient norms, and cosine similarity between the feature and supervised gradients.*

#### Gradient size and direction.

On real batches, we measure the gradient each feature loss sends to the encoder and compare it with the supervised gradient (Table 1). The gradients of the VkD variant and of CKA are both about $10^{3}$ times smaller than the supervised gradient, but they differ in direction. Both VkD gradients, with or without LayerNorm, are orthogonal to the task (cosine near zero), while CKA is the only feature loss with a consistent, weakly positive alignment, with a cosine of about $0.09$ . This small aligned part is what makes CKA trainable. The much larger orthogonal part is the structure that CKA adds to the representation, and Section 4.2 shows that it helps some languages and hurts others.

#### Ruling out limited capacity.

One explanation for the stalled projection loss is that a 640-dimensional student cannot represent the 1024-dimensional teacher features. This is not the case. The teacher features are low rank, and 640 dimensions capture about 99% of their energy across five languages. The optimizer simply does not follow this gradient. Consistent with this, the CKA between student and teacher features rises from 0.49 to between 0.83 and 0.87 under all three losses. The two VkD versions reach similar values although their gradients differ in size by about 200 times, so for VkD this alignment comes from the task loss rather than the feature loss.

#### Cost.

The projection is also expensive. The standard orthogonal parametrization rebuilds an orthonormal matrix in every forward and backward pass, which raises the feature cost per step by about $230\times$ , from 1.76 to 407 ms for six layers. CKA needs no projection, and a training step with CKA is about $2.8\times$ faster than with the projection loss (Figure 2c). It is therefore both the more effective and the cheaper choice, and we use it from here on.

### 4.2 CKA helps non-English languages and hurts English

We train a full run, called CKA in Table 2, that is identical to the Baseline except for a CKA term with $\lambda_{\text{feat}}{=}32$ . We chose this weight with a small sweep on a held-out set, not on the test sets. A large fixed weight works because the CKA loss shrinks as alignment improves; the VkD variant, in contrast, needed a decaying weight.

| System | EN-7 | ML-9 | Avg |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 9.85 | 7.24 | 8.55 |
| VkD variant | 10.18 | 7.22 | 8.70 |
| CKA | 11.25 | 6.83 | 9.04 |
| Lang-gated CKA | 11.21 | 7.18 | 9.19 |

*Table 2: Feature losses on top of the Baseline (WER after CA). Lang-gated CKA applies CKA to non-English frames only.*

CKA gives the best multilingual WER of all systems, 6.83% on ML-9, but the worst English WER, 11.25% on EN-7 (Table 2). The English degradation is significant (Appendix F) and appears late in training: English follows the Baseline early on and then drifts upward. English WER is noisy across checkpoints for every system (Section 7), but CKA adds a consistent upward shift.

We attribute this to the part of the CKA gradient that is orthogonal to the task (Section 4.1). On the non-English languages, where the student underfits, the teacher’s representation structure is a useful prior. On English, abundant data and logit distillation already give a strong signal, so this structure adds little, and its task-orthogonal part pulls the shared encoder away from what English needs. English is not at its limit at this size: the student still trails the teacher, and CAFE improves it once this pull is removed (Section 7). Whether feature distillation helps therefore depends on the language.

### 4.3 Why the trade-off is hard to fix at the loss level

If the gain and the harm were separable, a targeted change to the loss could keep the multilingual gain and drop the English harm. We examine three such changes, one in a training run and two with training-free probes. The trained one does not help, and the probes argue against gating and projection, pointing to the shared encoder as the cause.

Multilingual data dominates the CKA term. By sampling weight, English makes up 13.6% of training frames, 5.2% human-labeled and 8.4% pseudo-labeled, and the other languages 86.4%, mostly pseudo-labeled VoxPopuli. The CKA statistics are therefore computed mostly on non-English frames.

#### Remedy 1: Masking English in the loss.

Lang-gated CKA uses the true language labels to apply CKA to non-English frames only. However, as shown in Table 2, English WER stays as high as with plain CKA, at 11.21% versus 11.25%, and multilingual WER rises from 6.83% to 7.18%. Removing English frames from the loss does not stop the multilingual CKA gradient from changing the shared encoder weights that English also uses. It also discards English frames whose alignment signal was useful.

#### Remedy 2: Gating by the loss gap.

A language-agnostic option is to switch CKA off wherever the student has caught up with the teacher, measured by the loss gap $\Delta=\text{nll}_{S}-\text{nll}_{T}$ . A training-free probe on about 4000 utterances shows that the gap is positive almost everywhere (96% to 98% of utterances) and is not larger on English than on other languages. This holds on human-labeled data and late in training, when English is already degrading. The student is still behind the teacher on almost every utterance, so the task loss does not reveal the harm. The harm lies in the structure of the features.

#### Remedy 3: Subspace projection.

A third option is to remove from the CKA gradient its component in the subspace that English uses. For each distilled layer, we measure the share of the multilingual CKA gradient energy that falls inside the top- $k$ subspace of English activations,

$$ \text{overlap}(k)=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(U_{k}^{\top}G\,U_{k})}{\operatorname{tr}(G)}, $$

where $U_{k}$ spans the top- $k$ principal directions of English activations and $G$ is the second moment of the per-frame CKA gradient. English activations spread over most of the 640 dimensions, and the CKA gradient overlaps with their subspace by 97.5% to 99.5%, far above the chance level of about 81%. Projecting this part out would keep only a few percent of the CKA gradient, which amounts to removing CKA. The overlap stays stable during training. The multilingual gain and the English harm use the same encoder directions.

All three run into the same problem: all languages share one representation, and the CKA gradient comes mostly from multilingual data. The simplest fix consistent with this is to give the non-English side its own parameters. Lowering the CKA weight late in training is not a solution either, because nothing in the loss tells us when to do it.

## 5 Proposed CAFE: Confined-Adapter Feature Distillation

Since the trade-off is hard to separate in the loss, CAFE separates it in the parameters. It routes non-English utterances through a shared set of adapters and applies the feature loss only through them, so the feature gradient never reaches the shared encoder that English relies on, as shown in Figure 3. The CKA gradient thus reaches only the adapters, which only non-English utterances use.

#### Language-routed adapters.

At each distilled layer $\ell$ we insert one residual bottleneck adapter, shared by all non-English languages, with update

$$ A_{\ell}(x)=U_{\ell}\,\phi(D_{\ell}\,x), $$

with down projection $D_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}$ , up projection $U_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}$ , GELU nonlinearity $\phi$ , and rank $r$ . $U_{\ell}$ is initialized to zero, so $A_{\ell}$ starts at zero and the model at initialization is identical to the Baseline. The adapter is applied only to non-English utterances, through a per-utterance mask $m\in\{0,1\}$ ,

$$ \tilde{x}=x+m\,A_{\ell}(x), $$

so the outputs for English are bit-identical to those of the encoder without adapters. The adapters are the only language-dependent parameters, and the encoder remains a single multilingual model.

CAFE keeps the base recipe of Section 3 and changes only the feature term. CKA is computed between the adapted non-English features and the teacher features, with the same fixed $\lambda_{\text{feat}}$ . No schedule is needed, because the CKA loss shrinks as alignment improves.

#### Gradient confinement.

The CKA term trains the adapters to match the teacher, and a stop-gradient keeps its gradient out of the shared encoder, as shown in the blue panel of Figure 3,

$$ \Phi^{\text{CKA}}_{\ell}=\operatorname{sg}(x)+A_{\ell}(\operatorname{sg}(x)), $$

where $\operatorname{sg}$ is the stop-gradient operator. The supervised and logit losses update the shared encoder as usual. Confining the CKA gradient in this way has two consequences. First, the CKA term cannot affect English directly at any $\lambda_{\text{feat}}$ , because English bypasses the adapters and the shared encoder receives no CKA gradient. Second, the CKA weight does not need to be lowered late in training, because the task gradient keeps the adapters close to the task optimum. To account for the added parameters, we also train a control named Capacity that has the same adapters but no feature loss.

## 6 Experimental Setup

#### Training.

The student encoder has 24 layers of dimension 640, against 1024 for the teacher22 2 https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3. All runs share the same data, optimizer, and schedule: AdamW with Noam annealing (base scale 3.0, peak learning rate ${\approx}1.2\times 10^{-3}$ , 10k warmup steps) for 350k steps on NVIDIA H100. Batches are formed dynamically by duration with up to 22 s of audio per GPU, with 3 gradient accumulation steps. Logit distillation uses $\lambda_{\text{logit}}{=}5$ and $\tau{=}2$ . The feature distillation is applied at layers ${\{3,7,11,15,19,23\}}$ . The CAFE adapters have rank $r{=}64$ .

#### Data.

The student is trained on about 116.9 million utterances (564k hours) in 25 languages from 10 corpora, mostly VoxPopuli, YODAS, Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS), and Libri-Light (Wang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023; Pratap et al., 2020; Kahn et al., 2020). VoxPopuli, YODAS, and Libri-Light use the Granary pseudo-labels (Rao Koluguri et al., 2025). English is the largest language by hours (35%), but sampling reduces it to 14% of training frames. We evaluate on 48 held-out test sets (296k utterances, 24 languages): the public Open ASR Leaderboard33 3 https://huggingface.co/spaces/hf-audio/open_asr_leaderboard, whose EN-7 sets are English short-form and whose ML-9 sets come from FLEURS (5) and MLS (4), plus the larger multilingual Common Voice v25 (Ardila et al., 2020) and Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS-8) test sets. Detailed data statistics are in Appendix C.

#### Model selection.

Checkpoints are saved every 6k steps, and CA averages the last 7. The ranking holds for windows of 5, 7, and 10 checkpoints (Table 10). CA smooths the fluctuation between consecutive checkpoints at no extra training cost. It is widely used in ASR Shinayama et al. (2026); Zhou et al. (2024); Gaido et al. (2024); Lam et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2024) and other speech-related tasks Alastruey et al. (2024); Li et al. (2026a); Liu et al. (2025); Zhu et al. (2025).

#### Systems.

We compare four 25-language systems in a $2\times 2$ design, with or without the adapters and the CKA term (Table 3). Baseline and CKA are the systems of Section 4, and Capacity has the same adapters as CAFE but no feature loss. CAFE versus Capacity thus isolates the confined CKA term, and Capacity versus Baseline isolates the adapters alone. CAFE w/o sg is identical to CAFE but without the stop-gradient, to test its effect. Baseline-8lang and CAFE-8lang are trained on the 8 languages of MLS, with a different seed.

#### Main result.

CAFE improves on the Baseline in English and multilingual WER: EN-7 falls from 9.85% to 9.03%, and ML-9 from 7.24% to 7.00%. The checkpoint means show the same order, so the gain is not a product of averaging. CAFE also beats the Capacity control on both, which reaches 9.67% on EN-7 and 7.34% on ML-9, and both English gains are significant (Appendix F). The adapters alone give only a small English gain, so the improvement comes from the confined CKA term rather than from the extra parameters. Plain CKA has the lowest multilingual WER but the worst English. Against Capacity, the confined CKA term still lowers ML-9, nearly as much as plain CKA gains over the Baseline.

#### Effect of the stop-gradient.

Removing the stop-gradient brings the English degradation back. CAFE w/o sg reaches 10.44% on EN-7, worse than the Baseline, while its ML-9 of 6.95% matches that of CAFE. Its English standard deviation across checkpoints is 0.69, close to that of plain CKA and twice that of CAFE. The stop-gradient thus protects English at almost no multilingual cost.

#### Replication on 8 languages.

We train a matched pair, Baseline-8lang and CAFE-8lang, on the 8 languages covered by MLS, otherwise identical to their 25-language counterparts. The results in Table 3 show the same pattern with less data: EN-7 WER is improved from 10.11% to 8.71%, and ML-9 from 6.62% to 6.53%. The effect is therefore not specific to the 25-language setup.

#### Adapter overhead.

Table 4 compares CAFE with the same model without adapters. The adapters lower throughput by about 2.0%–3.8% and leave latency and memory almost unchanged, so CAFE runs as fast as a standard transducer of its size. All efficiency numbers follow the single-GPU protocol in Appendix A.

#### Stability.

English WER varies across checkpoints for every 25-language system, but least for CAFE, with a standard deviation of 0.32, and most for the Baseline, with 0.82 as shown in Table 3. Confining CKA to the adapters both lowers English WER and more than halves this variation. As a result, CAFE’s WER changes little with the CA window (ablation in Appendix D).

#### Routing.

The adapters carry the multilingual gain and must be skipped for English. Applying them to every utterance raises EN-7 from 9.03% to 15.95%, and never applying them raises ML-9 from 7.00% to 8.04%. When the language is unknown, a small gate of 0.19% parameters that we release makes this choice at a cost of 0.05 points in average WER (Appendix E).

#### Training dynamics.

Figure 4 tracks test-set WER during training for the 8-language pair. Multilingual WER falls smoothly for both models and the two curves stay close, so CAFE does not cost multilingual accuracy. English behaves differently. In the second half of training, the Baseline oscillates strongly, with spikes above 14% WER, while CAFE stays lower, varies less, with a standard deviation of 0.62 versus 0.96, and keeps improving. #### Discussion.

The results agree with the analysis in Section 4. English bypasses the adapters and the shared encoder receives no CKA gradient, so English utterances contribute exactly the same losses in CAFE and in Capacity. The English gain over Capacity, from 9.67% to 9.03%, must therefore come through the shared parameters, which non-English data trains differently once CKA has shaped the adapters. The training curves support this: CAFE removes the late English drift seen in the Baseline. We therefore attribute the gain to less interference on the shared encoder late in training.

## 8 Conclusion

Feature distillation does not help uniformly. We used gradients to explain why feature distillation does not add to logit distillation in compact multilingual ASR. The projection-based gradient is orthogonal to the task. The CKA gradient is weakly aligned with it, lowering WER on non-English languages but raising it on English. Because this gradient overlaps almost entirely with the subspace English uses, masking the loss fails in training, and our diagnostics argue against gating or projecting it. Guided by this diagnosis, we proposed Confined-Adapter Feature distillation (CAFE), which confines the CKA gradient to language-routed adapters that English bypasses and so moves the fix from the loss to the parameters. CAFE improves on the Baseline mainly in English, with a smaller multilingual gain. It also beats an adapter-only control and more than halves the variation of English WER across checkpoints.

## Limitations

We initialize the student by structured pruning of the teacher. This is the standard way to build a compact student at this data scale, and prior work finds that it outperforms training from scratch (Zhang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026). Our findings therefore apply to how such models are trained in practice, and we limit our claims to this setting. Whether the same pattern holds under random initialization is left to future work.

Each configuration is trained once. Our ablations already need several full runs on 564k hours of data, and repeating each with several seeds is too costly. As a check, the 8-language pair uses a different seed and language set and shows the same pattern (Section 7). The significance tests in Appendix F also compare the 7 checkpoints behind each averaged model, which captures some variation within a run. We acknowledge that these checks give only partial evidence and do not fully replace a multi-seed study.

CAFE needs to know whether an utterance is English. The main results take this from the test set, but in practice the language may be unknown. We therefore release a small language gate with the model (Appendix E). It adds 0.19% parameters and raises the average WER from 8.02% to 8.07%, still well below the 8.55% of the Baseline.

## Ethical Statement

#### Data and privacy.

All training and evaluation corpora are public research datasets used under their licenses (listed in Appendix C). We collected no new data from human subjects and ran no annotation study. Speech can reveal speaker identity and other personal information, so we use only the released data, make no attempt to re-identify speakers, and follow each corpus’s official train and test splits. For Common Voice we also remove training clips that share an utterance, speaker, or transcript with the test set (Appendix C).

#### Fairness and intended use.

ASR quality is uneven across languages, accents, and dialects, and compact models can widen this gap. Our study addresses this directly: it aims to help languages with less data than English without degrading English. We report dialectal English (CORAAL) and per-language results so that differences stay visible rather than hidden in an average. Gaps remain, and performance on languages, accents, or domains outside our test sets is not guaranteed. The intended use is transcription for accessibility and for on-device and offline settings. Like any ASR system it can be misused, for example for surveillance, and should be deployed with consent and appropriate safeguards.

#### Compute and efficiency.

Training at this scale (48 H100 GPUs, 564k hours of audio) has a significant one-time energy cost. The resulting student is compact (254M parameters), fast, and uses little memory, so the recurring cost of inference, which dominates in deployment, is low. Distilling a small model from a larger teacher is partly a step toward efficiency and accessibility.

#### Usage of AI assistants.

AI language models were used in two capacities: (1) code debugging, and (2) language polishing during paper writing. All experimental design, model development, analysis, and scientific conclusions were made by the authors.

#### Hardware.

All timings are on a single NVIDIA H100 (80 GB). To account for run-to-run variation, we run the full measurement on three separate GPUs and report the mean.

#### Data.

We time on MLS-8. For each of the eight languages we draw 500 random test utterances (4000 in total), keeping only clips of at most 30 seconds, so that every model, including Whisper with its fixed 30-second window, runs on the same set. All clips are decoded to WAV in advance, so the timing includes only model computation. The same set is used for every model and GPU.

#### Metrics.

RTFx is the total audio duration divided by the total computation time (higher is better), reported at batch sizes 1 and 32. P50 latency is the median time per utterance at batch size 1 (lower is better). Peak memory is the maximum GPU memory used at batch size 32 (lower is better). All models run in the same code on the same data and batch sizes, so the numbers in Tables 4 and 6 are directly comparable.

## Appendix B Per-dataset results for external systems

Table 6 gives the per-dataset results behind Table 5. As in the main text, the goal is not to rank systems, since several external models cover far more languages (over 1600 for omniASR), which is a harder task. The goal is to show that our student and the teacher are competitive for their size. All systems, including the teacher, are decoded and scored with the same code and the official Open ASR Leaderboard text normalizer, applied to both hypotheses and references. The teacher’s SPGISpeech WER of 3.98% is close to that of external systems such as Whisper-medium at 2.92%, so a normalization mismatch does not explain the student’s higher SPGISpeech WER. On the English short-form sets, the gap between teacher and student varies by domain, from 0.55 points on LibriSpeech clean to 4.0 points on SPGISpeech, which points to training data coverage rather than model size (Appendix C).

The four shared MLS languages use the same audio in both groups. For the teacher, Whisper, and our models, the two groups come from separate batched bf16 runs, so padding changes a few greedy outputs. Systems evaluated later decode each shared set once. We report the results as measured rather than replacing them. The two runs differ by 0.02 WER points on average and at most 0.06, which changes no comparison in this paper.

#### Training languages.

Table 7 lists the 25 training languages by hours. English dominates (about 35%, 200k hours), followed by European languages at roughly 2 to 5% each and a tail of lower-resource languages. The imbalance between English and the other languages therefore comes from the data, not from our design.

Table 8 breaks the same data down by corpus. The left panel shows the two largest corpora, VoxPopuli and YODAS. The right panel shows MLS and Common Voice, followed by the English corpora. The total matches Table 7.

#### Test sets.

We combine the public Open ASR Leaderboard test sets with the larger multilingual Common Voice v25 (24 languages) and Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS-8) test sets. The English part draws on LibriSpeech (Panayotov et al., 2015), GigaSpeech (Chen et al., 2021), SPGISpeech (O’Neill et al., 2021), VoxPopuli (Wang et al., 2021), AMI (Carletta et al., 2006), TED-LIUM (Hernandez et al., 2018), Earnings-21 and Earnings-22 (Del Rio et al., 2021; Del Rio et al., 2022), and CORAAL (Kendall and Farrington, 2023); the multilingual part uses FLEURS (Conneau et al., 2023), MLS (Pratap et al., 2020), and Common Voice (Ardila et al., 2020). The four leaderboard MLS sets (es, fr, it, pt) use the same audio as the corresponding MLS-8 sets.

#### Test-set isolation.

No development or test data is used for training. For every corpus except Common Voice we follow the official splits. The official Common Voice train split is deliberately small, so we enlarge it with validated clips that the split leaves out. We then remove any clip that shares with a test example (i) its utterance ID, (ii) its speaker ID (client_id), or (iii) its transcript after lowercasing and whitespace normalization. The speaker and transcript checks are needed because Common Voice records the same sentence from many speakers. Removing only matching clip IDs would still let test sentences and test speakers into training. This keeps a large amount of otherwise unused audio while removing any utterance, speaker, or transcript overlap with the test set.

A wrong activation on English costs more than a missed one on other languages, so we tune the threshold on held-out training-corpus samples not used to train the gate. We select $\theta{=}0.8582$ and use it for all test evaluations and the released model. With the gate, the average WER rises by only 0.05 points, from 8.02% to 8.07%. ## Appendix F Significance testing

We test English, where the conflict we study appears, and the multilingual leaderboard sets. Each test compares two systems on the same utterances. At the utterance level we use a paired permutation test (10,000 draws), which swaps the outputs of the two systems on each utterance with probability 0.5, and a paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples within each test set) for the 95% confidence interval. Both use the same means as Table 3: the mean of per-set WER for EN-7, and for ML-9 the mean of the FLEURS and MLS means.
